clue.text: Boss making blunder right at the end

indicators.note: says the letter for right is placed after the blunder, closing the word

parts.note: a gaffe is a social blunder

explanation.surface: A manager makes a mistake just as things are finishing.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaffer is British slang for a boss or foreman, the person in charge at work.

clue.text: Gangster covered in blood abundantly

indicators.note: the gangster is wrapped by the blood, so his letters sit inside it

parts.note: gore is spilt, clotted blood
AL is Al Capone, the crossword's stock gangster

explanation.surface: A mobster ends up thoroughly bloodstained.
explanation.definitionFit: Placed after a noun, the adverb means in plenty, in great quantity.

clue.text: No way to receive the tradesman?

definitions.text: No way to receive the tradesman?

parts.words: No way to receive the tradesman?
parts.note: traditionally tradesmen called at the back or side entrance, never the main entrance of a house

explanation.walkthrough: Older British houses had a tradesmen's entrance at the back, so the main entrance at the street side was not where deliveries came.
explanation.definitionFit: The main entrance of a house is the one a visiting tradesman was not expected to use.

clue.text: Religious type before getting a bit of money

parts.note: ere is an old word meaning before
a mite is a tiny coin or sum, as in the widow's mite

explanation.surface: Someone devout used to be poor until a small sum came their way.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermit, especially a Christian recluse living apart for religious reasons, is this sort of devout person.

clue.text: Lady one's seen in pubs

indicators.note: the words for one's appear inside the word for pubs

parts.note: bars are pubs or drinking places
taken as written, the possessive giving its letters

explanation.surface: A woman of rank is spotted drinking in the local taverns.
explanation.definitionFit: A peeress is addressed as Lady, so the title holder fits the noble sense of the word.

clue.text: Is AB on hand working before onset of panic when this order's given?

definitions.text: Is AB on hand working before onset of panic when this order's given?

indicators.note: the shuffled letters come ahead of the next piece
working here means the letters are put to work in a fresh arrangement
the onset of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A sailor is on duty just before panic sets in, when the captain gives the order to leave the ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer: an AB (able seaman) on hand as panic begins is exactly when this order is given. 'working' shuffles IS AB ON HAND; 'onset of' takes the P of panic.
explanation.definitionFit: The command to evacuate a sinking vessel is given at a moment of rising panic aboard.

clue.text: The art of early plane manufacture?

definitions.text: The art of early plane manufacture?

parts.words: The art of early plane manufacture?
parts.note: a child's first aeroplane is usually folded from a sheet of paper, the Japanese paper-folding craft

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests aviation history; the planes are paper darts folded by children.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese craft of folding paper into shapes, including the classic paper aeroplane.

clue.text: What's boarded a vessel the wrong way with clipped wings? Duck!

indicators.note: the extracted letters are then read in the opposite direction
with its wings clipped the phrase loses its outer letters, leaving an inner run

explanation.surface: Someone climbs on board backwards with a damaged bird, and is told to get down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with clipped wings' strips the outer letters of 'boarded a vessel', leaving EDAVE among them; 'the wrong way' reads it backwards. 'What's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck a question or a blow is to dodge or avoid it.

clue.text: Copper full of energy participating in country watch

indicators.note: the filled policeman is placed within the word for country

parts.note: a state is a nation or country

indicators.note: the energy symbol sits inside the copper's letters

parts.note: PC is a police constable, a copper
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: An energetic policeman takes part in a national event as an observer.
explanation.definitionFit: To watch an event as an onlooker rather than take part is to be a spectator.

clue.text: Small room unruly adolescent once stole from

parts.note: the loo is the lavatory, often called the smallest room
a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a rebellious 1950s British youth

explanation.surface: A badly behaved teenager in the old days pilfered from a little room.
explanation.walkthrough: Teddy boys were 1950s British youths in Edwardian-style clothes, known for trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Plundered or robbed, past tense, as in the shops were ransacked.

clue.text: Fence lacking colour protecting one grave

indicators.note: the colourless word wraps around and shields the others

parts.note: pale means wan or lacking colour
I is the Roman numeral one
grave and sad both mean sombre or serious

explanation.surface: A drab barrier guards a single burial plot.
explanation.definitionFit: A palisade is a fence of pointed stakes forming a defensive enclosure.

clue.text: Rex, awfully tired around day before feast, recovered

parts.note: R stands for Rex, Latin for king

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round the next piece
awfully signals the word is mangled into another order

parts.note: an eve is the day before a festival, as Christmas Eve

explanation.surface: A man named Rex, exhausted on the eve of a celebration, got something back.
explanation.walkthrough: Rex looks like a man's name but gives R, Latin rex for king. 'awfully' rearranges the exhausted word into ETRID, and 'around' wraps it round the festival's eve.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrieved means got back or regained, a synonym of recovered.

clue.text: I put in chives and soys, stirring soup

indicators.note: stirring mixes the ingredients, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook adds herbs and soy to a pot, mixing it into a soup.
explanation.definitionFit: A creamy leek and potato soup served chilled, a classic of French-style cookery.

clue.text: Ace bloke for being representative

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for ace in cards
a gent is a man, a bloke

explanation.surface: A top-notch chap is chosen to speak for others.
explanation.definitionFit: An agent acts on behalf of someone else, a representative.

clue.text: It's trend of novice sadly to be cocksure

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Beginners these days tend to be far too sure of themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Too sure of oneself, brashly and excessively certain.

clue.text: London resident, he, as kind to drop 'h'?

indicators.note: dropping the letter h removes it from the first word, as Cockney speech does

parts.note: taken as written before losing its h
taken as written
tender means gentle or kind

explanation.surface: A Londoner from the East End drops his aitches as a matter of course.
explanation.walkthrough: Semi-&lit: Cockneys of the East End traditionally drop the h sound. The East End is the working-class area of east London.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the East End, the traditional working-class district of east London.

clue.text: Secure as cat before secret has been divulged?

definitions.meaning: certain to be won, as good as done

definitions.text: as cat before secret has been divulged?
definitions.meaning: letting the cat out of the bag means revealing a secret, so before that the cat is still inside

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means secured or certain, and literally where the cat stays until the secret escapes.

clue.text: _______ with 'bursary' in certain poetry

definitions.meaning: the blank is a word that rhymes with bursary, so the answer read as a sentence says that word rhymes with it
a specific type of verse, traditional children's rhymes

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as a sentence: the first word, a room for children, rhymes with 'bursary', filling the blank.
explanation.definitionFit: Traditional short verses sung or recited to young children are a particular kind of poetry.

clue.text: Serious listener needing cosy spot

parts.note: an ear is the organ that listens
a nest is a snug, comfortable place

explanation.surface: A grave hearer longs for a comfortable corner.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnest means sincere and grave in intention, a synonym of serious.

clue.text: Graduate female (educated) beginning to languish in marriage

parts.note: an MA is a Master of Arts, a graduate
Rita is the woman of the play and film Educating Rita

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A woman with a degree, well schooled, starts to wilt in her married life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'marriage' is used as a modifier, as in marriage guidance. Educating Rita is Willy Russell's play about a woman's education.
explanation.definitionFit: Used attributively, as in marriage vows, the noun matches the adjective relating to wedlock.

clue.text: Exist as CEO, top

parts.note: to be is to exist
a chief executive is the head of a company

explanation.surface: A man is content to be the chief executive at the top.
explanation.definitionFit: To top someone is slang for executing them, as cutting off the head does.

clue.text: That woman concealing yen quietly becomes over-excited

parts.note: her refers to that woman

explanation.surface: A woman who quietly hides her longing gets carried away.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyper is informal for wildly excited or overstimulated.

clue.text: US president leads a dance

parts.note: James K Polk was the 11th US president

clue.text: Replace what sounds like great garden-centre product

indicators.note: signals that the next phrase, spoken, gives the answer

parts.note: great is super and a seed is sold at garden centres, together super seed

explanation.surface: Something to swap in is a top-quality item from the nursery.
explanation.definitionFit: To supersede is to take the place of something older, to replace it.

clue.text: Something potentially lethal in news report

parts.note: a bullet can kill
taken as written

explanation.surface: A deadly item features in the news.
explanation.definitionFit: A short official statement of news, as broadcast on radio or television.

clue.text: Say, Dorothy's brought round some filling food!

parts.note: e.g. is short for for example, which say means
Dot is short for Dorothy, plus the possessive s

explanation.walkthrough: 'brought round' turns EGDOTS around as a whole.

clue.text: People receiving gift from member of family by river

parts.note: a gran is a grandmother
the Tees is a river in north-east England

explanation.surface: Recipients of a present from a relative living near the water.

clue.text: Bright old coin with name scratched out — old penny

indicators.note: the name's letter is erased from the coin

parts.note: a florin was a British two-shilling coin
D, from Latin denarius, was the symbol for the pre-decimal British penny

explanation.definitionFit: Florid means flushed red or showily colourful, so bright in a gaudy way.
